description: The sensory, short-term and long-term stores, with the coding, capacity and duration of each.
content_html:
The Multi-Store Model

Where does a memory go after you first encounter it? The multi-store model of memory proposes that information travels through three distinct stores: the sensory register, short-term memory, and long-term memory. Each store differs in how it codes information, how much it can hold (capacity), and how long it retains information (duration).

Key Fact

The multi-store model has three stores: the sensory register (large capacity, very brief duration), short-term memory (limited capacity of about 7 items, up to about 30 seconds), and long-term memory (potentially unlimited capacity, potentially permanent duration).

The Sensory Register

The sensory register receives information from all your senses simultaneously. It has a very large capacity — it can hold a huge amount of incoming sensory data — but its duration is extremely brief, lasting only fractions of a second. Most information in the sensory register is never processed further and simply fades away. Only information that is attended to moves on to short-term memory.

The coding in the sensory register matches the sense that detected it: visual information is coded visually (iconic memory), and auditory information is coded acoustically (echoic memory). Think of the brief afterimage you see when someone takes a flash photograph — that flicker of visual information is your iconic sensory register in action.

Short-Term Memory

Short-term memory (STM) holds information that is currently in use — for example, a phone number you have just read or the words in the sentence you are reading right now. STM has a limited capacity: research suggests around 7 items, plus or minus 2. Its duration is also limited — without rehearsal, information in STM lasts only around 15 to 30 seconds before it fades. The coding in STM is primarily acoustic — we tend to hold information as sounds in our head, even when we read written words silently.

Peterson & Peterson (1959) is the AQA named study for STM duration. Aim — to investigate the duration of STM without rehearsal. Method — participants were given a consonant trigram (e.g. CHJ) and immediately required to count backwards in threes from a given number to prevent rehearsal; recall was tested after intervals of 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 or 18 seconds. Results — recall fell sharply with time; after 18 seconds, recall dropped to approximately 5% of items. Conclusion — without rehearsal, STM duration is approximately 18–30 seconds.

Rehearsal is the key mechanism for transferring information from STM to long-term memory. By repeating or thinking about information, you keep it active in STM and eventually strengthen it enough to be stored long-term. Without rehearsal, information in STM decays and is lost. This is why repeating a phone number to yourself works — until you stop rehearsing, it stays available.

Long-Term Memory

Long-term memory (LTM) is the relatively permanent store for information that has passed through STM. Its capacity is thought to be essentially unlimited — there is no known upper bound on how much LTM can hold. Duration can be extremely long; people retain memories for their entire lifetime. The coding in LTM is primarily semantic — information is stored in terms of its meaning rather than its sound or appearance.

Key Fact

STM codes mainly acoustically, holds about 7 items (±2), and lasts up to around 30 seconds without rehearsal. LTM codes mainly semantically, has potentially unlimited capacity, and can last a lifetime.

A strength of the multi-store model is that it is supported by research. For example, Murdock’s serial position curve study (covered in the next lesson) provides evidence for the distinction between STM (recency effect) and LTM (primacy effect). The model also generates clear, testable predictions about coding, capacity and duration.

A weakness is that the model may be oversimplified. It treats STM and LTM as single, unitary stores, but later research suggests both are more complex. For instance, long-term memory is divided into episodic, semantic and procedural memory (as you saw in Lesson 1). The model also suggests rehearsal is the only route to LTM, but we know that emotionally significant events can enter LTM even without deliberate rehearsal.

How Information Moves Between Stores

Understanding the flow of information through the multi-store model is as important as knowing the features of each store. Information first reaches the sensory register automatically and simultaneously from all active sense organs. At any given moment, your sensory register holds a vast amount of information — every sound in the room, every patch of colour in your visual field, every sensation on your skin. Nearly all of this is never consciously attended to and fades within fractions of a second.

The gateway between the sensory register and STM is attention. When you selectively attend to a piece of incoming sensory information — for example, you hear your name mentioned in a noisy room — it is transferred into STM and becomes available for conscious processing. Everything else in the sensory register is lost without ever being consciously registered.

Once information is in STM, rehearsal determines whether it passes into LTM. Maintenance rehearsal — simply repeating information — keeps it circulating in STM. With sufficient repetition, the trace is strengthened enough to be stored in LTM as a more permanent memory. Without rehearsal, STM traces decay within about 30 seconds and are gone. This explains why you can forget a phone number almost immediately if you are interrupted before you dial it.

Not all information enters LTM only through deliberate rehearsal. Elaborative rehearsal — thinking deeply about meaning and linking new information to what you already know — is more effective than simple repetition. Emotionally significant events can also bypass ordinary rehearsal and enter LTM rapidly, which is why flashbulb memories (such as exactly where you were when you heard dramatic news) can be so vivid and lasting even without conscious rehearsal.
exam_tip_html: On questions about the multi-store model, make sure you can state the coding, capacity and duration for each of the three stores separately — examiners look for all three features. A common error is giving ‘acoustic coding’ for LTM when it is semantic, or forgetting the capacity limit of STM. For the 9-mark ‘describe and evaluate’ question, balance your time: describe each store with its features, then spend roughly the same time evaluating using both strengths (research support) and weaknesses (oversimplification, single unitary stores).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The multi-store model proposes three stores: sensory register (brief, large capacity), short-term memory (acoustic coding, ~7 items, ~15–30 seconds), and long-term memory (semantic coding, unlimited capacity, potentially permanent).
  • Rehearsal is the mechanism that transfers information from short-term to long-term memory; without it, STM traces decay and are lost.
  • The model has research support but is criticised for being oversimplified, treating each store as a single unitary system when both STM and LTM are now known to be more complex.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the main coding used in short-term memory?
A) Semantic
B) Visual
C) Acoustic
D) Tactile

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition stating that STM is the memory store that holds a limited amount of information (approximately 7 items) for a brief period (around 15–30 seconds), coded mainly acoustically.
Secure: Clear definition capturing limited capacity and brief duration.
Developing: Partial definition — may mention limited capacity or brief duration but not both.
Emerging: Vague attempt such as ‘memory that does not last long.’

practice_questions.text: Describe the features of the long-term memory store.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three features (coding = semantic, capacity = potentially unlimited, duration = potentially permanent/lifetime) described accurately with clear psychological language.
Secure: Two features described correctly with accurate terminology.
Developing: One feature described correctly; others missing or inaccurate.
Emerging: Vague response that does not use the terms coding, capacity or duration accurately.

practice_questions.text: Sasha reads a new phone number and keeps repeating it to herself until she can dial it. Use the multi-store model to explain what is happening in Sasha's memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies STM and rehearsal, explains that information entered STM (limited capacity, acoustic coding), and that Sasha is rehearsing to keep it active and potentially transfer it to LTM; clearly references the scenario.
Secure: Correct use of STM and rehearsal with reference to the scenario; explanation is clear.
Developing: Identifies STM or rehearsal but explanation is limited or only loosely linked to the scenario.
Emerging: Names a store without meaningful explanation or scenario engagement.

practice_questions.text: Describe the multi-store model of memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes all three stores (sensory register, STM, LTM) with coding, capacity and duration for each; explains how information flows between them via attention (sensory → STM) and rehearsal (STM → LTM); uses accurate terminology throughout.
Secure: All three stores described with most features correct; flow between stores mentioned.
Developing: Two stores described; one store or flow mechanism missing.
Emerging: Names the stores without describing their features or the flow of information.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the multi-store model of memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Three stores — sensory register (large capacity, brief duration, sense-specific coding), STM (acoustic coding, ~7 items, ~15–30 seconds), LTM (semantic coding, unlimited capacity, potentially permanent). Rehearsal transfers STM to LTM; information not attended to in sensory register is lost; information not rehearsed in STM decays.
Evaluation (AO3): Strength — supported by research evidence; Murdock’s serial position curve study provides evidence for separate STM and LTM stores. Weakness — oversimplified; STM and LTM are not single unitary stores (LTM has episodic, semantic and procedural divisions). Rehearsal as the only LTM transfer route is questioned — emotionally significant events can enter LTM without deliberate rehearsal.
Mastering: Accurate, detailed description of all three stores plus at least two developed evaluation points with elaboration.
Secure: Stores described and two evaluation points made with some elaboration.
Developing: At least two stores described; one evaluation point with limited elaboration.
Emerging: Brief description; evaluation absent or only one undeveloped point.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the approximate capacity of short-term memory?
How is information mainly coded in long-term memory?
Without rehearsal, information in short-term memory lasts approximately _____ seconds.
The process of repeating information to keep it in short-term memory or move it to long-term memory is called _____.
Match each memory store to one of its key features:
right: Very brief duration of fractions of a second

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three stores in the multi-store model of memory?
flashcard_questions.a: Sensory register, short-term memory, and long-term memory.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the coding of the sensory register?
flashcard_questions.a: Sense-specific: visual (iconic) or auditory (echoic), matching the incoming sense.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the capacity of short-term memory?
What is the duration of short-term memory without rehearsal?
What is the main coding used in short-term memory?
flashcard_questions.a: Acoustic — information is held as sounds.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main coding used in long-term memory?
flashcard_questions.a: Semantic — information is stored by meaning.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the capacity of long-term memory?
What is the duration of long-term memory?
flashcard_questions.a: Potentially permanent — can last a lifetime.

flashcard_questions.q: What process transfers information from short-term memory to long-term memory?
flashcard_questions.a: Rehearsal — repeating or thinking about the information.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to information in short-term memory that is not rehearsed?
flashcard_questions.a: It decays and is lost from the memory system.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one strength of the multi-store model.
flashcard_questions.a: It is supported by research evidence, such as Murdock's serial position curve study.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one weakness of the multi-store model.
flashcard_questions.a: It oversimplifies memory by treating STM and LTM as single unitary stores.

glossary_terms.definition: A model of memory that proposes information flows through three separate stores: the sensory register, short-term memory and long-term memory.
The first store in the multi-store model, which briefly holds incoming information from the senses before most of it is lost.
The memory store that holds a small amount of information for a brief period; information is mainly coded acoustically.
The process of repeating information to keep it in short-term memory or transfer it to long-term memory.
The memory store that holds large amounts of information for potentially very long periods; information is mainly coded semantically.

hero_image_caption: Like a filing system, the brain sorts information into stores of different durations.
